Prologue.

A doctor cannot properly apply medicines to a patient without first knowing what humor or cause produces the illness. Thus a good doctor must be learned in medicines and in diseases, so as to properly apply to each disease its contrary medicine. Preachers and confessors are doctors of souls, to cure spiritual diseases: it is fitting that they have knowledge of spiritual medicines and spiritual diseases. The preacher against the Vices of the Republic needs that knowledge to direct his doctrine against them, and the confessor needs it to know how to ask what is appropriate and to understand what is told to him in the exercise of his Office: it is very important that they know what is necessary to carry out their Offices. We ministers of conversion must not be careless, saying that among these people there are no more sins than simple-mindedness, fright, and trifles. For among them there are many very serious moral sins of the gravest kind. The sins of idolatry, rites and idolatries, and superstitions and sorceries, omens and abuses, ceremonies and idolatries: these have not yet been entirely eradicated. In order to preach against these things and even to know whether they still exist, one needs to know how they were practiced in the time of their idolatry: for want of knowing this, one fails to recognize many things and idolatries without understanding them. And some say in their excuse that these are mere trifles or childish things, not recognizing the root from which they spring, which is idolatry. And the confessors neither ask about them nor think that such things exist, nor do they know the language to ask about them, nor would they understand if they were told: so that the ministers of the gospel who will succeed those who first came to cultivate this new Vineyard of the Lord may not have cause to complain of their predecessors for having left the things of these native people in darkness. I, Fray Bernardino de Sahagún, professed friar of the order of my Seraphic father Saint Francis of the Observance, native of the town of Sahagún, at the command of the most Reverend Father, Fray Francisco Toral, provincial of this province of the Holy Gospel and Bishop of Campeche and Yucatán, have compiled books on the divine, idolatrous, human, and natural things of this New Spain. The first of these deals with the gods and goddesses that these native people worshipped. The second with the feasts with which they honored them. The third with the immortality of the soul and the places where they said souls went after leaving the bodies, and the suffrages and obsequies they performed for the dead. The fourth book deals with the judicial astrology that these native people used to know the fortune

Good or bad fortune that those born under certain signs would have. The fifth book deals with the omens that these native people used to divine things to come. The sixth book deals with the rhetoric and moral philosophy that these native people practiced. The seventh book deals with the natural philosophy that these native people understood. The eighth book deals with the lords and their customs and ways of governing the Republic. The ninth book deals with the merchants and other mechanical tradesmen, and their customs. The tenth book deals with the vices and virtues of the people in their own manner of living. The eleventh book deals with the animals and birds, and fish, and the species found in this land, and the trees, and herbs, and flowers, and fruits, metals, and stones, and other minerals. The twelfth book is entitled the Conquest of Mexico. These thirteen books, together with the grammar and appended vocabulary, were finished being drafted in the year one thousand five hundred and sixty-nine, though I had not yet been able to render them into Spanish nor add the Latin scholias and commentary to the work — I do not know what could be salvaged of it. In the year seventy that follows. From the said year until nearly the end of the year 1574, this work could not be extended further, due to the great harm that came from those who were supposed to support it. But when our Father Commissioner General of all these provinces of New Spain and Guatemala, of the order of our Seraphic Father Saint Francis of the Observance, arrived in this land, he ordered that all these books be translated into Spanish, and that both in Spanish and in the Mexican language they be written in a fair hand. This work is like a dragnet to draw out all the words of this language with their own proper and metaphorical meanings, and all their ways of speaking, and most of their ancient traditions, both good and bad. It will save a thousand efforts, because with much less labor than what remains for me here, those who wish to know could learn in a short time much of their ancient traditions and the entire language of this Mexican people. This whole work is very useful for knowing the worth of the Mexican people, which has not yet been recognized, because God cast over them that curse which Jeremiah, on behalf of God, hurled against his people — and so it ends saying thus.

Chapter Five. I will cause to come upon you, I will bring against you, a people from very far away: a very robust and forceful people: a very ancient people, skilled in battle, a people whose language you will not understand, nor have you ever heard their manner of speaking: all strong and spirited people, disposed to killing. This people will destroy you, and your women, and your children: and everything you possess: and will destroy all your towns and buildings. This has happened literally to these Indians, with the Spaniards: they were so overwhelmed and destroyed, they and all their things: that no appearance remained of what they once were. And so they are held to be barbarians, and people of the lowest taste: when in truth, in matters of governance, they surpass many other nations: who hold great pretension to being civilized: setting aside certain tyrannies which their manner of rule contained. And in this little that has been retrieved with great effort: the advantage is clearly apparent: what might have been shown, if everything could have been recovered. As regards the antiquity of these people: it is held as established, that for more than two thousand years, they have inhabited this land: which is now called New Spain. Because from their ancient paintings, there is knowledge: that that famous city, called Tula: was destroyed some thousand years ago, or very close to it: and before it was built, those who built it had many settlements in Tullantzinco: where they left many notable buildings: for in what time they were there, and in the time it took to build the city of Tula: and in how long it lasted in its prosperity: before it was destroyed, it is consistent with truth that more than a thousand years passed: from which it follows that at least five hundred years before the Incarnation of our Redeemer: this land was populated. This celebrated and great city of Tula: very rich, and of very wise and very forceful people, suffered the adverse fortune of Troy. The Cholultecs, who are those who escaped from it: have held the succession of the Romans: and as the Romans built the Capitol for their stronghold: so the Cholultans built by hand: that promontory which stands next to Cholula, which is like a mountain or great hill, and is entirely full of mines or caves within. Many years later, the Mexicans built the City of Mexico: which is another Venice, and they in knowledge and in governance, are another Venetians. The Tlaxcaltecs appear to have succeeded to the fortune of the Carthaginians. There are great signs of the antiquities of these peoples, as can be seen today in Tula and in Tullantzinco: and in a building called Xochicalco: which is on the borders of Cuernavaca. And in nearly all this land, there are signs and traces of very ancient buildings and objects. It is indeed a matter of great wonder: that God should have allowed, for so many centuries hidden, a forest of so many peoples and idolaters: whose abundant fruits only the devil has gathered: and in the fires of hell holds them stored. Nor can I believe, that the Church of God will not prosper: where the synagogue of Satan has had such prosperity: according to that of Saint Paul. Grace will abound, where

the crime abounded. Of the knowledge and wisdom of these people there is a reputation that it was great, as appears in book ten, where in chapter 29 it speaks of the first settlers of this land, affirming that they were perfect philosophers, astrologers, and very skilled in all the mechanical arts. Of fortitude, which among them was more esteemed than any other virtue, and through which they rose to the highest degree of valor: they had great exercises, as appears in many parts of this work. In what concerns the religion and worship of their gods, I do not believe there have been in the world idolaters so reverent of their gods, nor at such cost to themselves, as these people of New Spain. Neither the Jews nor any other nation bore so heavy a yoke, nor so many ceremonies, as these natives have maintained for so many years, as appears throughout this entire work. Regarding the origin of these people, the account given by the elders is that they came by sea from the direction of the north. And it is certain that they came in some vessels, of what manner they were built is not known, except that it is conjectured from a tradition among all these natives that they came out of seven caves, and that these seven caves are the seven ships or galleys in which the first settlers of this land came. According to plausible conjectures, the people who first came to settle this land came from the direction of Florida, traveling along the coast, and disembarked at the port of Panuco, which they call Panco, meaning the place where those who crossed the water arrived. These people came in search of the earthly paradise, and they carried as their name Tamoachan, which means "we seek our home," and they settled near the highest mountains they could find. In coming toward the south to seek the earthly paradise, they were not wrong, for it is the opinion of writers that it lies beneath the equinoctial line; and also that it is some very high mountain — in this too they were not wrong, for writers say that the earthly paradise lies beneath the equinoctial line and is a very high mountain whose peak reaches near the moon. It appears that they, or their ancestors, had some oracle concerning this matter, whether from God or the devil, or a tradition from the ancients that passed from hand to hand until it reached them. They sought what by human means cannot be found, and Our Lord God intended that the unpopulated land should be peopled, so that some of their descendants might come to populate the celestial paradise, as we now see by experience. But why do I linger recounting divinations? For it is most certain that all these peoples are our brothers, descended from the stock of Adam as we are; they are our neighbors, whom we are obliged to love as ourselves. Whatever they may have been in times past, we see by experience now that they are able in all the mechanical arts and practice them; they are also able to learn all the liberal arts and sacred theology, as has been seen by experience in those who have been taught these sciences. As for what they are in matters of war, experience has been had of them, both in the conquest of this land and in other particular conquests that have been carried out since then.

How strong they are in enduring hardship, hunger, thirst, cold, and lack of sleep; how quick and ready they are to face any dangerous situation. They are no less capable of Christianity, if in it they are properly cultivated. It certainly seems that in these our times, and in these lands, with this people, our Lord God has wished to restore to the Church what the devil had robbed from it in England, Germany, and France, in Asia and Palestine. For this we are greatly obliged to give thanks to our Lord, and to work faithfully in this his New Spain.

To the sincere reader.

When this work was begun, those who heard of it began to say that a Calepino was being made; and even now, many do not cease to ask me what terms the Calepino covers. Certainly, it would have been very useful to make a work as valuable for those who wish to learn the Mexican language as Ambrosio Calepino made his for those who wish to learn Latin and the meaning of its words. But certainly, there has been no opportunity for this, because Calepino drew his words, their meanings, their ambiguities, and their metaphors from the reading of the poets, orators, and other authors of the Latin language, authorizing everything he wrote with citations from those authors. That foundation has been lacking for me, because there are no letters or writing among this people, and so it was impossible for me to make a Calepino. But I have laid the foundations so that whoever wishes may make one with ease, because through my industry twelve books have been written in the proper and natural language of the Mexican tongue, wherein, beyond being very pleasing and profitable reading, one may also find all the ways of speaking and all the words that this language uses, equally authorized and verified, just as Virgil, Cicero, and the other authors authorized the Latin language. These twelve books are arranged so that each page has three columns: the first in the Spanish language, the second in the Mexican language, the third the explanation of the Mexican words, marked with their reference numbers in both parts. The Mexican language portion has been fully drafted in clean copy across all twelve books; the Spanish language and the annotations have not yet been done, because I have been unable to do more, for lack of help and support. If I were given the necessary assistance, in one year, or a little more, everything would be completed; and surely if it were finished, it would be a treasure for learning many things worthy of being known, and for easily learning this language with all its secrets — something of great value in both New Spain and Old Spain.

This book does not proceed by chapters, and therefore no summary is placed here; it proceeds by the letters of the alphabet, which indicate what is said in Latin or in Spanish, responding to what is said in the Mexican language. fol. 24.

First Book, which deals with the gods that the natives of this land worshipped, which is New Spain.

Chapter One, which speaks of the principal god whom the Mexicans worshipped and to whom they made sacrifices, called Huitzilopochtli.

This god, called Huitzilopochtli, was like another Hercules: he was most robust, of great strength, and very warlike — a great destroyer of towns and killer of peoples. In wars, he was like living fire, greatly feared by his enemies. The device he bore was a dragon's head, very frightening, that spat fire from its mouth. He was also a sorcerer or trickster, who transformed himself into various birds and beasts. The Mexicans held this man in great esteem during his lifetime on account of his strength and skill in war. After he died, they honored him as a god, and offered him slaves, sacrificing them in his presence. They sought that these slaves should be very well treated and very finely adorned with those ornaments they used — of goldwork and lip-plugs — doing this to honor him the more. Another like him lived in the region of Tlaxcala, who was called Camaxtli.

This one, like his vicar, was used when it was suddenly necessary to go out to meet the enemies: because then it was necessary that this Paynal — which means swift, hastened — should go out in person to rouse the people, so that in great haste they would go out to confront the enemies. And they believed that when he walked upon the earth, he stirred up enmities and discord, from which arose many hardships and troubles. They said that he himself incited some against others so that they would make war. And for this reason he was called Necoc Yaotl, which means: sower of discord on both sides. And they said that he alone governed the world, and that he alone gave prosperity and riches, and that he alone took them away whenever he wished. He gave riches, prospe-

The fourth chapter speaks of the god who was called Tlaloc tlamacazqui.

This god, called Tlaloc tlamacazqui, was the god of rains. They believed that he gave the rains to water the earth, and that through this rain all the grasses, trees, fruits, and provisions grew. They also believed that he sent hail, lightning, thunder, and storms of water, and the dangers of the rivers and the sea. In calling him Tlaloc tlamacazqui, the meaning is: that he is the god who dwells in the earthly paradise, and that he gives to men the provisions necessary for bodily life. The services that were rendered to him are in the second book, among the feasts of the gods.

The first of these goddesses was called Cihuacoatl. They said that this goddess brought adversities: poverty, degradation, hardships.
